meta.title: Reading and influences
meta.note: The order changes each day. Influence is not a syllabus, and learning is rarely linear.
meta.intro: A map of books, essays, institutions and voices I return to when the simple explanations stop working.

tiers.label: Start here
tiers.microCopy: A way in, not a conclusion.

items.name: Institute for Government
items.annotation: I return to it when I want to understand how government actually behaves under constraint, rather than how structures say it should behave.

items.name: Government Digital Service – Service Manual
items.annotation: Useful when discussion becomes too abstract. It brings the focus back to users, service outcomes and the practical discipline of delivery.

items.name: Nesta
items.annotation: I use Nesta when I want examples of innovation and systems change that sit somewhere between policy ambition and practical intervention.

items.name: Behavioural Insights Team
items.annotation: A useful counterweight to intuition. It keeps pulling change questions back towards observable behaviour, evidence and what actually shifts outcomes.

items.name: Thinking in Systems — Donella Meadows
items.annotation: I return to Meadows whenever an apparently simple intervention starts producing unexpected consequences elsewhere in the system.

tiers.label: Go deeper
tiers.microCopy: When the simple explanations stop working.

items.name: Oxford Review (open articles)
items.annotation: Useful when management language starts sounding too certain. It forces claims back towards evidence, quality of reasoning and what we actually know.

items.name: NIST AI Risk Management Framework
items.annotation: I return to NIST when AI discussion becomes too abstract. It forces the conversation back towards responsibility, risk and organisational controls.

items.name: Paul Graham – Essays
items.annotation: Useful less as doctrine than as provocation. The essays often expose assumptions about scale, power, ambition and the way people build things.

items.name: OECD – Digital Government and AI
items.annotation: A way to step outside local practice and compare how different systems approach digital government, capability and institutional responsibility.

items.name: The Fearless Organization — Amy Edmondson
items.annotation: I return to psychological safety when a change problem is being described as resistance, capability or communication but the deeper issue may be whether people feel safe to speak and learn.

items.name: Sensemaking in Organizations — Karl Weick
items.annotation: Useful when organisations are trying to act before the situation is fully understood. Weick helps explain how people construct enough meaning to move.

tiers.label: Challenge your assumptions
tiers.microCopy: This may change how you see the problem.

items.name: Complexity and Management (Emergence Journal)
items.annotation: A useful check against treating complexity as a fashionable metaphor. It asks whether the ideas survive contact with serious management practice.

items.name: AI Now Institute – Research
items.annotation: I return to AI Now for the questions technology discussions often skip: who has power, who bears the cost and who gets to define what progress means.

items.name: The Long Now Foundation – Ideas
items.annotation: A useful antidote to short-term organisational thinking. It widens the time horizon and makes consequences, stewardship and resilience harder to ignore.

items.name: Cory Doctorow – Pluralistic
items.annotation: I return to Doctorow when I want the incentive structure made explicit. The writing is sharp on power, lock-in, platform behaviour and institutional failure.

items.name: Adam Curtis – Documentary essays
items.annotation: The attraction is not that every argument is right. It is the way Curtis uses narrative, archives and juxtaposition to make systems of power visible.

items.name: London Review of Books – Essays
items.annotation: I value the willingness to stay with complexity for longer than a normal news cycle allows, and to let argument develop without forcing a neat conclusion.

items.name: Aeon Essays
items.annotation: Useful for reframing familiar questions. The best pieces shift the angle enough that an organisational problem stops looking inevitable.

items.name: The Atlantic – Technology & Ideas
items.annotation: I read selectively for long-form attempts to connect technology with institutions, society and behaviour rather than treating products as the whole story.
